sections.history: Annappanpettai lies on the northern side of the Kaveri, in the country of old Chola Nadu not far from Sirkazhi. In the Tevaram hymns the place is called Tirukkalikkamur, and the child-saint Sambandar sang its Lord, which makes the temple a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The old name Kalikamur is explained by the faithful as the town where Shiva removes the hardships of the age of strife, the kali yuga. Local accounts speak of a very early foundation, of a rebuilding in stone under the Cholas around the tenth century, and of renovation by the Marathas in later times. These dates come from temple tradition rather than firm inscriptions, but the shrine itself has stayed in unbroken worship for well over a thousand years.
sections.architecture: This is a small and unassuming temple, and it makes no claim to grandeur. It has no towering rajagopuram and no flagstaff; instead the visitor enters beneath a graceful arch at the gateway. Within, the sanctum of Sundareswarar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Azhagammai is honoured in her own shrine. Ganesha is worshipped here as Selva Siddhi Vinayaka, the giver of prosperity and success. One detail that visitors remember is the group of Navagrahas, the nine planetary deities, who stand upright without the animal mounts that usually accompany them in other temples.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that the sage Parasara, the father of Vyasa, came to this place to worship Shiva, and that the Lord granted him his vision here. The sage is said to have asked the Lord to remain with the people of the place, and Shiva agreed, abiding as Sundareswarar, the beautiful lord. The countryside was once thick with vilva trees, the leaf most dear to Shiva, and from this the Lord is also called Vilvavana Nathar, the lord of the vilva forest. The very name of the town carries a gentler promise: that those who come here in trouble will find the weight of the age lifted from them.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the rhythm of Shaiva worship through the year. Maha Shivaratri is observed with night-long worship, and the monthly Pradosham draws devotees in the evening hour sacred to Shiva. Utsavams follow the Tamil calendar and are celebrated by the villagers with simple devotion. Specific festival dates and processions are not recorded in the sources we could verify, so please confirm them locally, especially in the months of Masi and Panguni.
sections.experience: Come to Tirukkalikkamur for stillness rather than spectacle. The village is small and the temple smaller still, and a visit here is a slow, quiet one: pass beneath the arch, stand before Sundareswarar, then turn to Azhagammai in her shrine. Look for the Navagrahas standing without their mounts, and spend a few moments in the corridor with the hymns of Sambandar in mind. The temple is easily combined with the other Tevaram shrines scattered through the Sirkazhi countryside, and pilgrims often come here as one stop on a longer circuit of the northern Kaveri bank.

visit.timings: Reported as open for a short morning session and again from late afternoon until evening, roughly 8:00 to 10:00 and 5:00 to 7:30; village temples keep varying hours, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but not inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask the priest before photographing rituals or worshippers.
visit.gettingThere: Annappanpettai is about 14 km from Sirkazhi on the Sirkazhi to Thiruvenkadu road, by way of Mangaimadam, and town buses running from Sirkazhi towards Konaiyampattinam pass through the village. Sirkazhi and Mayiladuthurai are the nearest railway stations. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport, a long road journey away, so most pilgrims travel by road or rail from Sirkazhi.
